steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write a short introduction for our paper on GoLLIE, an LLM fine-tuned to follow annotation guidelines for zero-shot information extraction. Explain why IE is hard to transfer, why label names alone aren't enough for LLM-based zero-shot IE, and briefly present GoLLIE.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:

- LLM-based zero-shot IE and the limitation of label names
- Current LLMs don't follow annotation guidelines
- GoLLIE

steps.name: detailed_outline

  - SoTA performance depends on amount of human-annotated data; model learns guidelines from examples

- LLMs for zero-shot IE
  - LLM advances (cite) -> generalization to unseen tasks
  - zero-shot IE systems use LLM knowledge to annotate new examples (cite)
  - pre-training gives strong representation of person/organization -> can be prompted to extract them
  - limitation: schemas define "person" differently; ACE05 (cite) counts pronouns as persons, CoNLL03 (cite) does not
  - IE needs annotation guidelines, not just label names
- LLMs fail to follow guidelines

  - Figure 1: domain-specific zero-shot NER; gpt-3.5-turbo prompted with guidelines (cite) ~20 F1 on Music or Politics
  - high-performance zero-shot IE with less human annotation still open
- GoLLIE
  - Guideline-following Large Language Model for IE
  - LLM fine-tuned to attend to guidelines, small set of well known IE tasks
  - zero-shot evaluation: outperforms SoTA (cite) (Figure 1)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Information Extraction (IE) is a very challenging task. You can see this in the detailed guidelines that human annotators have to follow to do the task, which have granular definitions and many exceptions. How well current SoTA models perform depends a lot on how much human-annotated data there is, because the model learns the guidelines from these examples. But performance drops a lot when they are tested on a new annotation schema. To get good results, the common practice in IE is to manually annotate every new domain and schema from scratch, since there is almost no transfer between application domains. Unfortunately this is unfeasible, both in financial cost and in human effort.

Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLM) have made it possible to build models that generalize to unseen tasks. So current zero-shot IE systems use the knowledge encoded in LLMs to annotate new examples. Because of the pre-training process, models now have a strong representation of what a person or an organization is, so they can be prompted to extract mentions of these categories from a text. But this has a clear limitation: not every annotation schema defines ”person” (or any other label) the same way. For example, ACE05 annotates pronouns as persons, but CoNLL03 does not. IE tasks need more information than just the label names; they need annotation guidelines.

- LLMs fail to follow guidelines
  - instruction-following LLMs fail on annotation guidelines out of the box
  - Figure 1: domain-specific zero-shot NER; gpt-3.5-turbo prompted with guidelines (cite) ~20 F1 on Music or Politics
  - high-performance zero-shot IE with less human annotation still open

- GoLLIE
  - Guideline-following Large Language Model for IE
  - LLM fine-tuned to attend to guidelines, small set of well known IE tasks
  - zero-shot evaluation: outperforms SoTA (cite) (Figure 1)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Information Extraction (IE) is a very challenging task. You can see this in the detailed guidelines that human annotators have to follow to do the task, which have granular definitions and many exceptions. How well current SoTA models perform depends a lot on how much human-annotated data there is, because the model learns the guidelines from these examples. But performance drops a lot when they are tested on a new annotation schema. To get good results, the common practice in IE is to manually annotate every new domain and schema from scratch, since there is almost no transfer between application domains. Unfortunately this is unfeasible, both in financial cost and in human effort.

Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLM) have made it possible to build models that generalize to unseen tasks. So current zero-shot IE systems use the knowledge encoded in LLMs to annotate new examples. Because of the pre-training process, models now have a strong representation of what a person or an organization is, so they can be prompted to extract mentions of these categories from a text. But this has a clear limitation: not every annotation schema defines ”person” (or any other label) the same way. For example, ACE05 annotates pronouns as persons, but CoNLL03 does not. IE tasks need more information than just the label names; they need annotation guidelines.

Current LLMs are trained to follow instructions, but out of the box they fail to follow annotation guidelines. For example, Figure 1 shows results on domain-specific zero-shot Named Entity Recognition. When gpt-3.5-turbo is prompted with guidelines, the results are low, around 20 F1 score on the Music or Politics domains. It is still an open challenge to build a system that does high-performance zero-shot information extraction and reduces the dependence on expensive human annotations.

In this work we present GoLLIE (Guideline-following Large Language Model for IE), an LLM that is fine-tuned to learn how to attend to the guidelines on a small set of well known IE tasks. A comprehensive zero-shot evaluation shows empirically that GoLLIE does better than the SoTA in zero-shot information extraction (see Figure 1).

To get good results, the common practice in IE is to manually annotate every new domain and schema from scratch, since there is almost no transfer between application domains. Unfortunately this is unfeasible, both in financial cost and in human effort.

Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLM) [2] have made it possible to build models that generalize to unseen tasks. So current zero-shot IE systems use the knowledge encoded in LLMs to annotate new examples [3,4]. Because of the pre-training process, models now have a strong representation of what a person or an organization is, so they can be prompted to extract mentions of these categories from a text. But this has a clear limitation: not every annotation schema defines ”person” (or any other label) the same way. For example, ACE05 [5] annotates pronouns as persons, but CoNLL03 [6] does not. IE tasks need more information than just the label names; they need annotation guidelines.

Current LLMs are trained to follow instructions, but out of the box they fail to follow annotation guidelines. In this work we present GoLLIE (Guideline-following Large Language Model for IE), an LLM that is fine-tuned to learn how to attend to the guidelines on a small set of well known IE tasks. steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The task of Information Extraction (IE) is highly challenging. This is evident in the detailed guidelines, with granular definitions and numerous exceptions, that human annotators must follow to perform the task. The performance of current SoTA models depends heavily on the quantity of human-annotated data, as the model learns the guidelines from these examples. However, performance decreases significantly when tested on a new annotation schema [1]. The common practice in IE to achieve good results is to manually annotate each new domain and schema from scratch, as almost no transfer exists across application domains. Unfortunately, this is unfeasible, both in terms of financial cost and human effort.

Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLM) [2] have enabled models capable of generalizing to unseen tasks. Thus, current zero-shot IE systems leverage the knowledge encoded in LLMs to annotate new examples [3,4]. As a by-product of pre-training, models now possess a strong representation of what a person or an organization is, and can therefore be prompted to extract mentions of those categories from a text. However, this has a clear limitation: not every annotation schema defines ”person” (or any other label) in the same way. For example, ACE05 [5] annotates pronouns as persons, while CoNLL03 [6] does not. IE tasks require more information than just label names; they require annotation guidelines.

Current LLMs have been trained to follow instructions, but they fail to follow annotation guidelines out of the box. For instance, Figure 1 shows results on domain-specific zero-shot Named Entity Recognition. The results of gpt-3.5-turbo when prompted with guidelines [7] are low, around 20 F1 score on the Music or Politics domains. Building a system that enables high-performance zero-shot information extraction while reducing the dependence on costly human annotations remains an open challenge.

In this work, we present GoLLIE (Guideline-following Large Language Model for IE), an LLM fine-tuned to learn how to attend to the guidelines on a small set of well known IE tasks. A comprehensive zero-shot evaluation empirically demonstrates that GoLLIE outperforms the SoTA [4] in zero-shot information extraction (see Figure 1).
